supply-s2.title: Four events for the furniture workshops of Larkfield
supply-s2.text:
Larkfield is an invented town where small workshops make wooden chairs. Four things happen over one year:

  1. A storm closes forests in the region and the price of lumber jumps.
  2. Workshops start using a new laser cutter that halves the time it takes to shape each chair.
  3. The town starts paying each workshop \$20 for every chair it produces.
  4. Workshop owners hear that chair prices will rise sharply next month.

items.q: Label the axes and the curve of a market supply graph for bicycles.

why.correct: Price goes on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. The upward-sloping curve is supply, S: sellers offer more bicycles at higher prices.

items.q: The price of flour, the main input for bread, rises. Shift the right curve in the market for bread.

why.correct: A higher input price raises the cost of making each loaf, so bakers offer fewer loaves at each price: supply shifts left.

key.because: a rise in the price of an input (flour)

slips.D: Flour is an input for sellers; its price changes the cost of making bread, which shifts supply, not demand.

items.q: A new robot lets solar panel makers assemble each panel in half the time. Shift the right curve in the market for solar panels.

why.correct: Better technology lowers the cost of producing each panel, so makers offer more at each price: supply shifts right.

slips.D: The robot changes how panels are made, not how many buyers want, so supply shifts.

items.q: Half of the ferry companies on a lake go out of business and sell their boats abroad. Shift the right curve in the market for ferry rides on the lake.

why.correct: Fewer sellers means fewer rides offered at each price, so market supply shifts left.

items.q: The price of laptops falls and nothing else changes. Mark the point on the supply curve that shows the new price and quantity supplied.

why.correct: A change in the good's own price moves sellers along the same supply curve. A lower price means a smaller quantity supplied: the point moves down and to the left.

items.q: If Fennel Farm and Ridge Farm are the only sellers, what is the market quantity supplied at \$4 a box?

why.correct: Market supply adds every seller's quantity at the same price: $20 + 20 = 40$ boxes.

mistakes.why: That is one farm's quantity. Market supply adds both farms at \$4.
That is the market quantity at \$3. Read the \$4 row.

items.q: The market price of strawberries rises from \$3 to \$5 a box. What happens in the market?
options: Supply shifts right from 30 to 50 boxes
Quantity supplied falls from 50 to 30 along the curve
Quantity supplied rises from 30 to 50 along the supply curve
Supply shifts left because buyers pay more

why.correct: A change in the good's own price moves sellers along supply. The market quantity supplied rises from 30 to 50 boxes; supply itself does not shift.
options: A change in the own price does not shift supply.
That is the change for a price fall from \$5 to \$3.
Right: the own price changed, so sellers move along the curve.
What buyers pay does not move the sellers' curve.

items.q: When the price rises from \$4 to \$5, which farm adds more boxes, and how many?
options: Ridge Farm, 6 more boxes
Fennel Farm, 4 more boxes
Both add 5 more boxes
Ridge Farm, 26 more boxes

why.correct: Fennel Farm goes from 20 to 24 (4 more) and Ridge Farm from 20 to 26 (6 more), so Ridge Farm adds more.
options: Right: from 20 to 26.
Fennel adds 4, fewer than Ridge's 6.
They add different amounts: 4 and 6.
26 is Ridge's quantity at \$5, not the change.

items.q: A third farm starts selling at the market and offers 10 boxes at each price from \$2 to \$5. What happens to market supply?
options: Quantity supplied rises along the same curve
It shifts left as the farms split the buyers
It does not change unless the price changes
It shifts right by 10 boxes at each price

why.correct: Market supply sums the sellers' quantities at each price. The new farm adds 10 boxes at each price, so the market supply curve shifts right.
options: A movement along supply needs a change in the own price.
More sellers raise supply; buyers are on the demand side.
The number of sellers is a supply shifter.
Right: one more seller adds to the sum at each price.

items.q: Event 1: the price of lumber jumps. What happens to the supply of chairs?
options: Supply shifts right
Supply shifts left
Quantity supplied rises along the curve
Demand for chairs shifts left

why.correct: Lumber is an input. A higher input price raises the cost of each chair, so workshops offer fewer chairs at each price: supply shifts left.
options: Costlier inputs make each chair more expensive to produce.
Right: a higher input price lowers supply.
The chair price did not change; an input price did.
Lumber is an input for sellers, so supply changes.

items.q: Event 2: workshops start using a laser cutter. What happens to the supply of chairs?
options: Supply shifts left
Supply shifts right
Quantity supplied falls along the curve
Demand for chairs shifts right

why.correct: Better technology lowers the cost of producing each chair, so workshops offer more chairs at each price: supply shifts right.
options: A faster way to make chairs makes producing them cheaper.
Right: better technology raises supply.
The price of chairs did not change.
The cutter changes how chairs are made, not how many buyers want.

items.q: Event 3: the town pays workshops \$20 for every chair they produce. What happens to the supply of chairs?
options: Supply shifts left
Demand for chairs shifts right by \$20
Nothing changes until buyers react
Supply shifts right

why.correct: A payment for each unit produced works like a lower cost per chair, so workshops offer more at each price: supply shifts right.
options: A payment per chair makes producing more attractive, not less.
The payment goes to sellers, not buyers.
Sellers respond to the payment directly.
Right: a payment per chair acts like a lower cost.

items.q: Event 4: owners expect chair prices to rise next month. What happens to the supply of chairs this month?
options: Supply this month shifts left
Supply this month shifts right
Quantity supplied this month rises along the curve
Demand this month shifts left

why.correct: Sellers who expect a higher price later hold some chairs back to sell then, so they offer fewer this month: supply this month shifts left.
options: Right: sellers hold stock back for the higher price.
A higher expected price makes waiting to sell more attractive.
This month's price did not change; expectations did.
The event is about sellers' expectations.

items.q: Which statement is the law of supply?
options: A higher price lowers the quantity sellers offer
Supply rises when buyers' incomes rise
Other things equal, a higher price raises the quantity supplied
Sellers offer more when input prices rise

why.correct: The law of supply: other things equal, when a good's price rises, the quantity supplied rises, and when it falls, the quantity supplied falls.
options: That is backward: sellers offer more at a higher price.
Income is a demand shifter.
Right: price and quantity supplied move together.
Higher input prices lower supply.

items.q: A bakery already uses its ovens all day. To bake more bread it must pay workers overtime and rent a second oven. Why does this make the supply curve slope up?
options: Buyers want fewer loaves when the price rises
Overtime shifts the supply curve to the right
A higher price lowers the bakery's costs
Each extra loaf costs more, so a higher price is needed to offer more

why.correct: Producing more costs more for each extra loaf (overtime, a rented oven), so the bakery offers more loaves only at a higher price that covers that rising cost.
options: That is the law of demand, a buyer's choice.
Overtime makes extra output costlier; it does not raise supply.
The price does not change the cost of baking.
Right: the price must cover the rising cost of extra output.

items.q: A farmer can plant corn or soybeans on the same land. The price of soybeans rises sharply. What happens to the farmer's supply of corn?
options: It shifts right because farming pays more
Quantity of corn supplied rises along the curve
It shifts left as land moves to soybeans
It does not change because corn's price is the same

why.correct: Soybeans are another good the same land can produce. When soybeans pay more, the farmer switches land to them, so she offers less corn at each price: the supply of corn shifts left.
options: Only soybeans pay more; corn now uses land that could earn more elsewhere.
The price of corn did not change.
Right: the price of another good the seller can make rose.
The price of a related good the seller can produce shifts supply.

items.q: Which changes would shift the supply of phone cases to the right? Select all that apply.
options: The price of the plastic used in cases falls
The price of phone cases rises
Ten new case makers start selling online
Wages for the workers who make cases rise

why.correct: Supply shifts right when sellers offer more at each price: cheaper inputs, better technology and more sellers all do it. A higher price of phone cases is a movement along supply.
options: Right: a cheaper input raises supply.
A change in the own price is a movement along supply.
Right: more sellers raise market supply.
Higher input costs lower supply.

items.q: Over one year, the number of bubble wrap sellers stays the same, but each one offers 500 fewer rolls at every price. What has happened?
options: Quantity supplied has fallen along the curve
Supply has decreased: the curve shifted left
Supply has increased: the curve shifted right
Demand has decreased: the demand curve shifted

why.correct: Less offered at every price is a decrease in supply: the supply curve shifts left. A movement along the curve needs a change in the price of bubble wrap.
options: A movement along supply happens at a new price, not at every price.
Right: less is offered at each price.
Fewer rolls at each price is a decrease.
The change is in what sellers offer.
